title: Matrix Chain Multiplication Order
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Choosing parenthesization of a matrix product by DP minimises scalar multiplications in O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space.
short: Try every split point for every interval of matrices.
long: Try every split point for every interval of matrices. The number of possible parenthesizations is Catalan, so DP gives an exponential saving.
proof: The last multiplication splits the chain at some k, so an optimal solution combines optimal solutions of the two sides.
consequence: It is the textbook example of interval DP and optimal substructure.

title: Interval Scheduling Greedy Choice
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Sorting intervals by finish time and accepting each compatible one maximises the number of scheduled intervals in O(n log n) time.
short: Finishing early leaves the most room for the rest.
long: Finishing early leaves the most room for the rest. Weighted interval scheduling instead requires dynamic programming.
proof: The earliest-finishing interval can be part of some optimal schedule by exchange, after which the same argument applies to compatible intervals.
consequence: It is the simplest nontrivial greedy scheduling algorithm.

title: Huffman Coding Greedy Optimality
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Repeatedly merging the two least frequent symbols produces an optimal prefix code in O(n log n) time with a priority queue.
short: Give short codes to frequent symbols by merging rare ones first.
long: Give short codes to frequent symbols by merging rare ones first. The resulting tree minimises expected code length for the given frequencies.
proof: The two least frequent symbols can be made deepest siblings in some optimal tree, reducing the problem to a merged symbol.
consequence: It is the classic application of greedy algorithms and heaps to data compression.

title: Alpha-Beta Pruning in Game Trees
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Alpha-beta pruning skips branches that cannot affect the minimax decision, reducing explored nodes to about b^{d/2} with good move ordering.
short: Stop searching a branch once it cannot change the answer.
long: Stop searching a branch once it cannot change the answer. Without good ordering the improvement can vanish; the bound is for ideal ordering.
proof: Maintaining alpha and beta bounds at ancestors allows cutoffs when a child's value exceeds the current bound.
consequence: It roughly doubles the depth reachable by game-playing programs.

title: Competitive Analysis of Online Algorithms
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: An online algorithm is c-competitive if its cost is at most c times the optimal offline cost plus a constant for every request sequence.
short: Compare against an adversary that knows the whole future.
long: Compare against an adversary that knows the whole future. It is the standard performance measure for caching, paging and scheduling under uncertainty.
proof: The ratio is taken as the supremum over all admissible request sequences.
consequence: It provides guarantees when probabilistic input models are unavailable.

title: Adversary Arguments for Lower Bounds
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: An adversary lower bound constructs inputs adaptively so that any algorithm must spend a certain number of operations before it can be correct.
short: Force the algorithm to inspect enough of the input.
long: Force the algorithm to inspect enough of the input. The unsorted-search bound and comparison-sort bound can both be phrased adversarially.
proof: The adversary keeps at least two consistent inputs indistinguishable until enough queries distinguish them.
consequence: It is a flexible tool for proving impossibility results.

title: Las Vegas versus Monte Carlo Algorithms
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Las Vegas algorithms always give a correct answer with random running time, while Monte Carlo algorithms have bounded running time with a small probability of error.
short: Randomise the time or randomise the correctness.
long: Randomise the time or randomise the correctness. Randomised quicksort is Las Vegas; Rabin–Karp with a random modulus is Monte Carlo.
proof: The distinction follows from which of time and correctness is guaranteed with probability one.
consequence: It guides algorithm selection when failure probability matters.

title: Pseudopolynomial Time and Strong NP-Hardness
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: An algorithm is pseudopolynomial if it is polynomial in numeric input values but not in the number of bits encoding them, as with O(nW) knapsack DP.
short: Large numbers encoded in few bits can break the bound.
long: Large numbers encoded in few bits can break the bound. A problem strongly NP-hard has no pseudopolynomial algorithm unless P = NP.
proof: W requires log W bits, so an algorithm linear in W is exponential in the input length.
consequence: It clarifies why some NP-hard problems admit practical DP while others do not.

title: NP-Hard versus NP-Complete
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: A problem is NP-hard if every problem in NP reduces to it; it is NP-complete if it is also in NP.
short: NP-completeness adds verifiability to hardness.
long: NP-completeness adds verifiability to hardness. Optimisation problems such as TSP are typically NP-hard but not formally NP-complete.
proof: The definitions differ only in the membership requirement in NP.
consequence: It determines whether a problem can be certified quickly as well as being hard.

title: Polynomial-Time Reductions
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: A polynomial-time many-one reduction maps instances of A to instances of B in polynomial time so that x is in A iff f(x) is in B.
short: Solving B efficiently would solve A efficiently.
long: Solving B efficiently would solve A efficiently. Reductions are the tool for transferring hardness and algorithms between problems.
proof: Composing an algorithm for B with the reduction yields an algorithm for A.
consequence: They define NP-hardness and structure the map of computational difficulty.

title: Fixed-Parameter Tractability
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: A problem is fixed-parameter tractable with parameter k if it can be solved in f(k) poly(n) time for some computable f.
short: Confine exponential work to a small parameter.
long: Confine exponential work to a small parameter. Vertex cover is FPT with k the cover size; kernelisation and branching are standard techniques.
proof: An algorithm meeting the form is by definition FPT, independent of n in its exponential part.
consequence: It provides a positive algorithmic theory for problems that are NP-hard in general.

title: PSPACE and Space Complexity
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: PSPACE is the class of decision problems solvable with a polynomial amount of memory, regardless of running time.
short: Memory, not time, is the scarce resource.
long: Memory, not time, is the scarce resource. By Savitch's theorem, PSPACE equals NPSPACE up to a quadratic blow-up in space.
proof: The class is defined by Turing machines with polynomial space bounds.
consequence: It captures games and quantified formulas where time may be exponential.

title: Time-Space Tradeoffs in Algorithms
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Many algorithms exchange memory for speed, as when a DP table gives O(1) lookup per state while a rolling array saves space but loses reconstructability.
short: Keeping more information usually speeds up queries.
long: Keeping more information usually speeds up queries. Hirschberg's algorithm recovers an LCS with linear space at the cost of extra recursive time.
proof: Storing intermediate results avoids recomputation, reducing time at the cost of memory cells.
consequence: Memory limits often dictate which algorithm variant is usable.

title: Information-Theoretic Lower Bounds
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: If an algorithm's answers distinguish N possible inputs, each yes/no query yields at most one bit, so at least log2 N queries are needed.
short: Count how many possibilities must be ruled out.
long: Count how many possibilities must be ruled out. This yields the log n bound for searching and the n log n bound for sorting permutations.
proof: A depth-d binary decision tree has at most 2^d leaves, so 2^d >= N implies d >= log2 N.
consequence: It turns counting arguments into rigorous impossibility results.

title: Ski Rental Competitive Ratio
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Buying skis after renting for exactly B days achieves competitive ratio 2 for the ski rental problem, and randomisation improves it to e/(e-1).
short: Wait until rentals would equal the purchase price.
long: Wait until rentals would equal the purchase price. It is the simplest benchmark problem in online decision making.
proof: If skiing stops before B days the cost matches OPT; otherwise rentals plus purchase are at most twice OPT.
consequence: It illustrates competitive analysis against an all-knowing offline optimum.

title: Work and Span of a Parallel Computation
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Work W is total operations and span S is the longest dependency chain; on p processors Brent's bound gives time at most W/p + S.
short: Divide work by processors, but dependencies set a floor.
long: Divide work by processors, but dependencies set a floor. Efficiency is W/(p T_p); a large span limits scalability.
proof: Greedy scheduling performs at most W/p work per step in parallel and cannot finish before the critical path S completes.
consequence: Work and span replace plain running time in parallel algorithm analysis.

title: Element Distinctness Lower Bound
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Deciding whether n real numbers are all distinct requires Omega(n log n) comparisons in the algebraic decision tree model.
short: Even yes/no uniqueness needs sorting-like work.
long: Even yes/no uniqueness needs sorting-like work. The bound motivated the algebraic decision tree model as a generalisation of comparison trees.
proof: The input space has Theta(n!) connected components corresponding to orderings, and each comparison tree leaf can cover only one.
consequence: Hashing gives expected linear time for discrete keys but not in the comparison model.

title: Concentration of Randomised Quicksort
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Randomised quicksort's running time is O(n log n) with high probability, not merely in expectation.
short: Bad pivot sequences are extremely unlikely.
long: Bad pivot sequences are extremely unlikely. Tail bounds follow from concentration of the number of comparisons, a sum of weakly dependent indicator variables.
proof: Azuma's inequality or bounded-differences arguments bound the deviation of comparison count from its expectation.
consequence: Randomised algorithms can offer robust probabilistic performance guarantees.

title: Smoothed Analysis of Algorithms
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Smoothed analysis measures running time on inputs obtained by slightly perturbing arbitrary instances, explaining why algorithms with bad worst cases often work well.
short: Between worst case and average case lies a realistic model.
long: Between worst case and average case lies a realistic model. The simplex method has polynomial smoothed complexity, in contrast to exponential worst-case examples.
proof: Perturbation limits how long an adversarial construction can survive, bounding the expected number of pivot steps.
consequence: It bridges theory and practice for numerics and local-search heuristics.

title: Iterated Square-Root Recurrence
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The recurrence T(n) = T(sqrt n) + O(1) solves to Theta(log log n).
short: Repeated square roots shrink n doubly exponentially fast.
long: Repeated square roots shrink n doubly exponentially fast. After k steps the argument is n^{1/2^k}, which becomes constant once k is about log2 log2 n.
proof: Set n_k = n^{1/2^k}; taking logs gives log n_k = (log n)/2^k, so k = log log n reaches a constant.
consequence: It appears in analysis of some union-find and integer algorithms.

title: Fenwick Tree Prefix Sum Queries
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A Fenwick tree stores at index i the sum of the range (i - lowbit(i) + 1)..i, where lowbit(i) is the largest power of two dividing i.
short: Overlapping power-of-two blocks encode prefix sums.
long: Overlapping power-of-two blocks encode prefix sums. It uses a single array of size n and supports prefix sums in O(log n) time.
proof: Repeatedly subtracting lowbit(i) decomposes [1..i] into disjoint stored blocks.
consequence: Fenwick trees are a compact alternative to segment trees for prefix-sum workloads.

title: Fenwick Point Update and Prefix Query
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Adding delta at position i means adding it to bit[j] for j = i, i + lowbit(i), ...; querying the prefix sum walks j = i, i - lowbit(i), ...
short: Indices climb for updates and descend for queries.
long: Indices climb for updates and descend for queries. Both loops visit at most log2 n entries, and the tree is built in O(n log n) or O(n) by a direct pass.
proof: Each update changes exactly the stored blocks containing i, and each query sums exactly the blocks covering the prefix.
consequence: It is the standard dynamic cumulative-frequency structure.

title: Fenwick Range Sum by Difference of Prefixes
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A range sum on a Fenwick tree is prefix(r) - prefix(l-1), costing O(log n).
short: Two prefix queries give any interval.
long: Two prefix queries give any interval. Two Fenwick trees can instead support range updates with point queries in O(log n).
proof: Prefix sums are additive over the difference of the two index ranges.
consequence: It makes Fenwick trees usable for general range sum problems.

title: Fenwick versus Segment Tree
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Fenwick trees are smaller and faster for invertible prefix aggregates such as sums, while segment trees support arbitrary associative operations and range updates on general intervals.
short: Specialised simplicity versus general flexibility.
long: Specialised simplicity versus general flexibility. Fenwick trees need an inverse operation to subtract prefixes; segment trees work for min, max and custom monoids.
proof: Fenwick blocks are fixed by index arithmetic; segment-tree nodes correspond to arbitrary intervals of the recursion.
consequence: Choose Fenwick for sums and frequencies, segment trees for min/max and lazy updates.

title: Segment Tree for Range Aggregation
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A segment tree stores an associative aggregate for each dyadic interval of an array, with leaves holding single elements.
short: A balanced binary tree over array intervals.
long: A balanced binary tree over array intervals. It supports point updates and range queries in O(log n) time for any associative operation.
proof: Any query interval decomposes into O(log n) canonical tree nodes.
consequence: Segment trees generalise Fenwick trees to min, max, gcd and custom monoids.
